actions.name: Review CPAP device download/compliance report
actions.result: Download for the past 30 nights: used 12 of 30 nights (40%), average use on nights used 2 h 10 min, average leak 38 L/min (large), residual AHI 14/hr, median pressure 10 cmH2O on auto-CPAP range 6-14 cmH2O. (Detailed nightly chart available for the most recent 14 nights shows a similar intermittent pattern, with usage on roughly half of nights.)

actions.name: Review clinic vitals from today's visit (reported by patient/home cuff)
actions.result: BP 146/90 mmHg, HR 82 bpm, home pulse oximetry on room air 95%, weight 258 lb, height 5'10", BMI 36.

actions.name: Camera inspection of mask fit and skin
actions.result: Full-face mask visualized on camera; patient has a moderate beard along the jawline and cheeks where the mask seal sits; mild redness over nasal bridge, no open skin breakdown.

actions.name: Camera inspection of humidifier chamber and tubing
actions.result: Humidifier chamber is bone dry with no water lines/residue visible; tubing has a small amount of dust; no visible mold.

actions.name: Ask patient to demonstrate donning mask and show headgear adjustment on camera
actions.result: Patient dons mask; straps are overtightened at the top (red strip marks on forehead), loose at the lower straps, consistent with air leak toward the eyes.

actions.name: Administer Epworth Sleepiness Scale today and compare to baseline
actions.result: Baseline Epworth Sleepiness Scale score at CPAP start was 14/24 (consistent with excessive daytime sleepiness). Re-administered today: current score 12/24, a modest improvement but still in the excessive-sleepiness range, which is inconsistent with adequate therapy given the poor adherence and high residual AHI on download.

actions.name: Review sleep study (diagnostic PSG) report
actions.result: Diagnostic polysomnography: AHI 38 events/hr (severe OSA), oxygen saturation nadir 79%, supine-predominant.

actions.name: Administer fatigue risk / drowsy driving screening tool (e.g., Epworth-based occupational risk screen)
actions.result: Structured fatigue-risk screening administered. Patient endorses borderline-high risk score consistent with excessive daytime sleepiness in safety-sensitive settings; score alone is non-diagnostic and does not specify any particular incident. Further direct, private conversation recommended to explore occupational safety concerns.

actions.name: Review current CPAP equipment order/prescription on file
actions.result: Order on file: Auto-CPAP, full-face mask size medium, pressure range 6-14 cmH2O, heated humidifier ordered but setting not documented as adjusted since setup.

actions.name: Assess bed partner report of symptom change
actions.result: Patient reports wife says his snoring has improved and she has moved back into their shared bedroom.

actions.name: Visual check of CPAP machine settings display on camera
actions.result: Device display shows humidifier heat setting at 'Off'; ramp time set to 20 minutes; current pressure range 6-14 cmH2O auto mode confirmed.

facts.chart: Patient presents for scheduled 6-week CPAP follow-up after starting therapy for severe OSA.
facts.says: They told me to check in since I've had this machine for about six weeks now.

facts.chart: Reports wearing CPAP 'pretty much all night' every night.
facts.says: I wear it pretty much all night, every night. I'm doing what I'm supposed to.

facts.chart: Reports ongoing fatigue and daytime sleepiness since starting therapy, though somewhat improved from before.
facts.says: I still feel pretty tired a lot of the day, maybe a little better than before but not great.

facts.chart: Reports his snoring has improved since starting CPAP, per bed partner report.
facts.says: My wife says I don't snore nearly as much anymore.

facts.chart: On discussion, reports he frequently wakes to find the mask pulled off during the night, without recalling removing it.
facts.says: Honestly, a lot of mornings I wake up and the mask is just... off. I don't even remember taking it off.

facts.chart: Describes air leaking from the mask seal toward his eyes, which he attributes to his beard interfering with the seal.
facts.says: Sometimes air blows right into my eyes, especially on the side with my beard. It's annoying.

facts.chart: Reports waking with a dry mouth most mornings.
facts.says: My mouth is bone dry most mornings, like I've been breathing through sandpaper.

facts.chart: On direct question, admits he has never filled the humidifier chamber with water since setup.
facts.says: Oh, that little water tray thing? I never actually put water in it. Nobody really explained I needed to.

facts.chart: Reports a sensation of panic or smothering shortly after donning the mask each night, described as claustrophobia.
facts.says: The first fifteen, twenty minutes with that thing on my face, I just feel like I'm suffocating. It freaks me out.

facts.chart: Expresses embarrassment about struggling with the CPAP machine and not wanting to seem like he is failing at treatment.
facts.says: I feel kind of dumb, like everyone else just puts it on and it's fine, and I can't even do that.

facts.chart: Reports his wife has moved back into their shared bedroom since his snoring improved with CPAP.
facts.says: My wife actually moved back into our room a couple weeks ago since I quieted down some.

facts.chart: Works full-time as a forklift operator, typically day shift, in a warehouse setting.
facts.says: I drive a forklift down at the warehouse, been doing that for about fifteen years.

facts.chart: Reports a near-miss episode about one month ago in which he nearly fell asleep while operating a forklift at work; no injury or collision occurred.
facts.says: About a month back I almost dozed off on the forklift for a second. Scared me pretty good, but nothing happened.

facts.chart: Expresses fear that reporting sleepiness-related safety concerns could put his job at risk.
facts.says: I can't afford to lose this job over something like that, so I haven't told anybody at work.

facts.chart: Denies morning headaches.
facts.says: No, I don't wake up with headaches or anything like that.

facts.chart: Denies chest pain or palpitations.
facts.says: No chest pain, no racing heart feeling, nothing like that.

facts.chart: Diagnosed with hypertension about 2 years ago, on lisinopril 10 mg daily.
facts.says: I've had high blood pressure for a couple years now, I take a pill for it every morning.

facts.chart: Reports taking lisinopril as prescribed without missed doses.
facts.says: I take that blood pressure pill every single morning with my coffee, never miss it.

facts.chart: Reports gradual weight gain over the past several years, no recent rapid change.
facts.says: I've put on weight slowly over the years, nothing sudden lately.

facts.chart: Drinks 2-3 cups of coffee daily, mostly in the morning.
facts.says: I have a couple cups of coffee in the morning to get going.

facts.chart: Drinks beer occasionally on weekends, 1-2 cans, no daily use.
facts.says: Maybe a beer or two on a Saturday watching the game, that's about it.

facts.chart: Denies current or past tobacco use.
facts.says: Never smoked, never liked the idea of it.

facts.chart: Was fitted with a full-face mask at setup; reports no one discussed alternative mask styles with him.
facts.says: They just gave me the one that covers my whole face. Nobody really talked about other options.

facts.chart: Reports his father also had loud snoring and was told he 'stopped breathing' at night but was never formally diagnosed or treated.
facts.says: My dad used to snore something awful too, my mom always said he'd stop breathing, but he never saw anybody about it.

facts.chart: Reports no episodes of drowsy driving in his personal vehicle, though acknowledges feeling tired on longer drives.
facts.says: I haven't nodded off driving my own truck or anything, just feel tired sometimes on long drives.

facts.chart: States he wants the therapy to work because he is worried about his long-term health and being around for his grandchildren.
facts.says: I want this to work. I've got grandkids now and I want to be around and sharp for them.

facts.chart: Denies chronic nasal congestion or allergies.
facts.says: My nose isn't stuffy or anything, breathing through it is usually fine when I'm awake.

facts.chart: Reports he wipes down the mask cushion occasionally but does not follow a regular cleaning schedule for the tubing or water chamber.
facts.says: I wipe the mask off every once in a while, I'm not real consistent about cleaning the rest of it.

facts.chart: Denies leg swelling.
facts.says: My legs look normal to me, no swelling that I've noticed.

facts.chart: Hopes to feel more rested during the day and to avoid health problems related to untreated sleep apnea.
facts.says: I just want to feel more awake during the day and not have this turn into something worse down the road.

facts.chart: Reports he received a brief setup demonstration from the equipment company but no follow-up troubleshooting call since initial delivery.
facts.says: The guy from the equipment company showed me how to turn it on and that was pretty much it. Nobody's called to check in since.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states he wears the CPAP 'pretty much all night' every night.
mismatches.recordEvidence: CPAP download report shows use on only 12 of 30 nights (40%), averaging 2 hours 10 minutes per night used, with the detailed 14-night chart confirming an intermittent, far-from-nightly pattern.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Self-reported adherence is often overestimated; always verify with objective device download data before coaching plans, and explore reasons for the gap non-judgmentally.

mismatches.patientClaim: Initially does not mention any workplace safety concerns and only discloses the forklift near-miss when asked directly and privately about drowsy driving/operating machinery.
mismatches.recordEvidence: High residual AHI (14/hr) and poor adherence pattern on the download, together with a borderline-high fatigue-risk screening score, are consistent with persistent excessive daytime sleepiness that could explain a safety-relevant near-miss episode, though neither the download nor the screening tool states any specific incident.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Objective sleepiness risk (poor adherence + high residual AHI + elevated fatigue-risk screen) should prompt direct, private screening for occupational and driving safety, since patients may fear disclosing safety incidents due to job security concerns, and such incidents only surface through genuine rapport-building conversation, not a chart lookup.

objectives.text: Accurately interpret CPAP device download data (usage percentage, average nightly hours, leak rate, residual AHI) and reconcile it with the patient's self-report of adherence.
Identify and troubleshoot modifiable barriers to CPAP adherence, including mask seal/leak related to facial hair, mouth/nasal dryness from an unused humidifier, and claustrophobia.

Use a non-diagnostic fatigue-risk screening tool to identify elevated sleepiness-related safety risk, then build rapport and ask direct, private, sensitive questions in conversation to elicit any occupational safety concerns and the patient's fear of job loss as a barrier to disclosure.

Recognize when findings (severe residual OSA with inadequate therapy, safety-relevant sleepiness) exceed respiratory therapy scope and require escalation/communication to the sleep medicine physician and, as appropriate, counseling about occupational safety reporting.
Provide patient-centered education and coaching on mask refitting/alternative interfaces, humidifier use, and desensitization strategies for claustrophobia to improve adherence.
Demonstrate respectful, stigma-free communication when discussing embarrassment, body habitus (BMI), and equipment struggles, maintaining therapeutic rapport while gathering accurate data.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Suboptimal CPAP adherence (40% nights used, average 2h10min/night) with large mask leak and elevated residual AHI (14/hr) in a patient with severe OSA, driven by identifiable, modifiable barriers: full-face mask leak related to facial hair, unused humidifier causing dryness, and mask-related claustrophobia; complicated by an undisclosed safety-relevant sleepiness episode at work.
differential: Inadequate CPAP therapy due to poor adherence/leak (most likely explanation for persistent daytime sleepiness)
Residual OSA requiring pressure/mode or mask reassessment by sleep medicine if adherence barriers are corrected and symptoms persist
Hypertension potentially related to untreated/undertreated OSA
Simple fatigue from shift work or lifestyle factors (less likely given clear device data)
keyFindings: CPAP download: 40% nights used, average 2h10min/night, large leak (38 L/min), residual AHI 14/hr
Patient self-report of near-full nightly use conflicts with objective download data
Humidifier chamber visibly dry/never filled; heat setting off
Mask leak toward eyes attributed to beard interfering with full-face mask seal
Reported claustrophobic/panic sensation in first 15-20 minutes of use
Near-miss drowsy episode while operating a forklift at work, previously undisclosed due to fear of job loss
BP 146/90 and BMI 36 at today's visit, consistent with ongoing cardiometabolic risk
plan: Review and discuss CPAP download data transparently with patient to align objective adherence with his perception
Troubleshoot mask seal: consider refitting, trial of alternative mask style (e.g., nasal mask/pillow or beard-compatible full-face interface), and strap adjustment coaching
Instruct patient to fill and properly use the heated humidifier chamber; adjust heat setting to address dryness
Coach gradual desensitization technique for claustrophobia (daytime wear, short sessions before sleep, ramp feature use)

Counsel patient on the safety significance of the near-miss drowsy episode; strongly encourage him to inform his employer per workplace safety policy and discuss with his sleep medicine physician/PCP; provide guidance on resources if available

Communicate findings (adherence barriers, residual AHI, safety near-miss) to supervising sleep medicine physician/DME team; this is outside RT scope to independently resolve residual AHI via prescription changes
Schedule close follow-up (e.g., 2-4 weeks) to recheck download data after interface and humidification changes
redFlags: Excessive daytime sleepiness with a safety-relevant near-miss operating machinery at work
High residual AHI (14/hr) despite therapy, suggesting inadequately treated severe OSA
Elevated blood pressure (146/90) potentially related to undertreated OSA, warrants communication with PCP/sleep medicine
educationPoints: CPAP effectiveness depends on both adequate nightly duration of use and a well-sealed mask interface; partial use with large leak can leave residual AHI high despite 'wearing' the device.
Facial hair can significantly affect full-face mask seal; alternative interfaces or seal strategies should be discussed rather than assuming nonadherence is purely behavioral.
Heated humidification is a standard adjunct that reduces dryness-related discomfort and can improve tolerance and adherence; it must actually be filled and powered to help.
Claustrophobic reactions to CPAP are common and treatable with desensitization strategies, mask trials, and ramp settings rather than being a reason to abandon therapy.

Patients may underreport safety-relevant sleepiness symptoms due to fear of job or income loss; creating a private, nonjudgmental space for direct questioning is essential for patient and public safety.

Respiratory therapists play a central role in device troubleshooting and coaching but should escalate residual disease severity, safety concerns, and prescription-level decisions to the supervising sleep physician.

scenario.studentBrief: You are a respiratory therapy student conducting a telehealth 6-week CPAP follow-up visit with Stefan Jovanovic, a 51-year-old man who started auto-CPAP therapy for severe obstructive sleep apnea (diagnostic AHI 38/hr, oxygen nadir 79%). The device download and today's vitals are already in the chart. Your job is to review his equipment data, assess how therapy is going, troubleshoot any barriers to use, and provide coaching.

profile.summary: "This case portrays a 51-year-old man six weeks into CPAP therapy for severe OSA who reports near-full adherence but whose device download reveals poor usage, large leak, and elevated residual AHI. It teaches respiratory therapy students to reconcile patient self-report with objective device data, troubleshoot common modifiable barriers (beard-related mask leak, unused humidifier, claustrophobia), and sensitively screen for and escalate a hidden occupational safety concern (near-miss drowsy episode on a forklift) within the bounds of RT scope of practice."
